source_read: PDF (version of record), Drug Alcohol Depend 82, pp. 168-176 (all 9 pages read in a pdftotext extraction; every number used checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi: pp. 169-174 including Tables 1-6 and Figures 1-2)

claims.overstatement: Slight, in one phrase: the paper says only rodents were used and that MOST of the animal studies gave the pre-treatments by injection (p. 174), not all; some gave antioxidants before and after MDMA. Smaller points: the paper glosses the comedown as the acute recovery period (p. 169), not 'the days after'; the paper reports no validation of its questionnaire rather than saying it was not validated; how often the listed strategies (Table 4) were used was not asked (p. 173), but how often people tested pills and preloaded or postloaded was asked (pp. 171-172). Understated: the magnitude lists the reasons 45.5%, 32.7% and 18.2% but leaves out the third most common, increasing the pleasurable effects of ecstasy, 21.8% of the 55 (Table 6), which shows that pre- and postloading were not only protective in intent (a finding about motives, to be stated without naming products or amounts if used).
claims.note: Every number in the statement and magnitude that comes from this source matches the printed text and tables (checked on the rendered pp. 169-174). Recomputed: ever tested 100 - 61.2 = 38.8% (45 of 116; summing the five categories gives 38.7% because of rounding), same as the editors' figure; preloaders 48 and postloaders 55 of 116; changed use 61 of 116 = 52.6%; the chi-squares reproduce from the printed percentages (preloading by more than 50 occasions 29/53 against 19/63, chi2 7.16; postloading 32/53 against 23/63, chi2 6.58; postloading by monthly use 33/59 against 20/55, chi2 4.38). 'About 30 tests': 10 listed variables x 3 outcomes (changed use, preloading, postloading) = 30, alpha 0.05 (0.025 when non-normal), no correction; gender differences were also tested and reported only if significant (p. 170), so 30 is a minimum. Editors' interval: +/-9 points is right for whole-sample shares (41.4% of 116: +/-9.0; 47.4%: +/-9.1), but shares among the 46 and 54 who listed products and the 55 who gave reasons carry about +/-12 to +/-14 points (5-HTP before 41.3% of 46, Wilson 28.3-55.7%; comedown 45.5% of 55, 33.0-58.5%). 'Harm-reduction websites': the paper says an ecstasy-related website and e-newsletter (p. 169); the acknowledgements name RaveSafe's e-newsletter and the Pill Reports website (p. 175), and RaveSafe is described as a harm reduction organisation (p. 169), so the wording is fair. Response rate: 98 questionnaires were handed out through acquaintances, the web route has no denominator and the split of the 116 by route is unknown (pp. 169, 175), so no response rate can be computed, as the claim says. No dosing or potentiation content in the claim; the 5-HTP and serotonin-syndrome lines report findings and the authors' caution only.

anchors.extracted: Australian residents aged 18 or over who had ever used ecstasy; data collected June to December 2004 by (1) convenience and snowball sampling among people known to the researchers (98 questionnaires handed out) and (2) an advertisement with a downloadable questionnaire on an ecstasy-related website and e-newsletter; returns were anonymous, so how many came by each route is unknown.

Self-administered questionnaire of about 15 minutes with closed and open questions in four sections; strategies were endorsed from a list separately for avoiding (a) negative side effects, (b) the comedown and (c) brain damage or neurotoxicity; pill-testing frequency, whether people had heard of and engaged in pre- and postloading, how often, and (open-ended) which products and why. No validation or piloting is reported.
116 questionnaires returned; 51.3% female; age 18 to 41, mean 26.5 years (SD 5.6); 82.5% Australian born; 50.4% from Victoria.

anchors.locator: Table 4 and 3.4 Harm reduction, 3rd paragraph (left column)
anchors.extracted: All 116 endorsed at least one strategy against negative side effects (no strategy 0.0%): drinking water 95.7%, limiting the amount of ecstasy 70.7%, breaks or chilling out 62.1%, healthy lifestyle 59.5%, vitamins or natural products 52.6%, other illegal drugs 30.2%, prescription medications 15.5%, pill testing 20.7%. No strategy: 4.4% for the comedown, 18.1% for neurotoxicity; about 30% used other illicit drugs against side effects and comedown.

anchors.locator: 3.4 Harm reduction, 2nd paragraph (p. 171 right column, continues p. 172 left column); Discussion p. 174, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Pill testing for MDMA or other substances: never 61.2%, rarely 16.4%, a quarter of the time 6%, half 1.7%, three quarters 8.6%, always 6% (45 of 116 ever, 38.8%, by subtraction; summing categories 38.7%). Discussion: about 40% had tested, only 6% always.

anchors.locator: 3.4 Harm reduction, 4th paragraph (right column) and Table 5
anchors.extracted: 65.5% had heard of pre- and postloading; 41.4% had preloaded and 47.4% postloaded. Preloading products (n = 46): multivitamins 50.0%, 5-HTP 41.3%, magnesium 23.9%, fruit or juice 23.9%; postloading (n = 54): 5-HTP 46.3%, multivitamins 44.4%, fruit or juice 24.1%. Products came via the internet 34%, supermarket 32.1%, pharmacy 30.2%.

Reasons for pre- or postloading (n = 55): reduce comedown 45.5%, reduce brain damage or neurotoxicity 32.7%, increase the pleasurable effects of ecstasy 21.8%, reduce negative side effects 18.2%, prevent fatigue or illness 14.5%.

53% had changed their use in response to dislikes; among these 61: decreased frequency 68.9%, decreased amount per occasion 16.4%, stopped 13.1%, increased amount 3.3%. Changing use was more common after more than 50 occasions (65.4% against 42.9%, chi2(1, n = 115) = 5.80, p = 0.016).

anchors.locator: 3.3 Other substance use, 1st paragraph and Table 2
anchors.extracted: No respondent used only ecstasy; all had used at least one substance before, during or after ecstasy. Alcohol 91.4% before, 81.0% during, 60.3% after; amphetamines 60.3%, 65.5%, 45.7%; tobacco 48.3%, 62.9%, 45.7%; cannabis most common after (62.9%).

anchors.locator: 3. Results, last paragraph (left column, before 4. Discussion); 2.4 Data analysis (p. 170)
anchors.extracted: Preloading went with younger age (24.9 against 27.6 years, t(113) = -2.59, p = 0.011) and more than 50 occasions (54.7% against 30.2%, chi2(1, N = 116) = 7.16, p = 0.007); postloading with more than 50 occasions (60.4% against 36.5%, chi2 = 6.58, p = 0.01) and monthly or more frequent use (55.9% against 36.4%, chi2(1, n = 114) = 4.38, p = 0.036). Ten variables were compared for three outcomes with t and chi-square tests at alpha 0.05 (0.025 if non-normal), no correction for multiple tests (p. 170).

Representativeness cannot be determined: convenience sampling plus respondents who search ecstasy-related websites and may have a particular interest in harm reduction. How often respondents used the listed strategies was not asked.

anchors.locator: 4. Discussion, right column, 2nd and 4th paragraphs (continuing on p. 175)
anchors.extracted: Protective pre-treatment evidence is from animals: antioxidants given before and after MDMA, fluoxetine, and tryptophan or 5-HTP in rats; most of these studies gave the pre-treatments by injection and only rodents were used, so oral human pre- and postloading may be less effective. Efficacy was not studied (p. 169, 2.1 Aims).
Using ecstasy with other substances that augment serotonin (5-HTP, SSRIs, St John's wort) can cause serotonin syndrome, listed by symptoms; no case or outcome data from the sample.

Three limitations: retrospective self-report, cross-sectional data (associations only, not causes), and an unknown split of returns between the two recruitment routes. Advertised through the RaveSafe e-newsletter and the Pill Reports website; internal funds only.

key_findings.correction: Complete but for two categories the finding leaves out: a quarter of the time 6% and half the time 1.7% (p. 172); the six categories sum to 116 respondents (71, 19, 7, 2, 10, 7), ever 45 of 116 = 38.8%.

The paper says only rodents were used and that MOST of the animal studies it mentions gave the pre-treatments by injection (p. 174, Discussion 13th paragraph), not all; some gave antioxidants before and after MDMA (11th paragraph). Read: 'the protective evidence comes only from rodent studies, most with injected pre-treatments'. The same wording appears in the card's interpretation_gap.claimed and in the claim. Locators are right (Discussion 11th to 14th paragraphs, pp. 174-175).

reporting_issues.note: Recomputed: preloading frequency percentages fit 45 (13, 3, 9, 6, 14) and postloading 55 (11, 3, 7, 8, 26); the chi-square fits 48 preloaders (29 of 53 against 19 of 63). Probably missing answers rather than an error.
n = 101 (place of use, p. 170), 114 (frequency, p. 173), 115 (t(113) and chi-square for occasions, pp. 171, 173), 116 elsewhere.
Five significant results (p = 0.007, 0.01, 0.011, 0.016, 0.036); 30 x 0.05 = 1.5 expected by chance. The chi-squares reproduce as uncorrected tests (7.16, 6.58, 4.38, 5.80).

The Introduction itself calls Akram and Galt (1999) one of the few studies of harm-reduction practices among people who use ecstasy (p. 169); Akram and Galt sampled people using dance drugs generally, so the authors' claim may be meant narrowly, but as written it conflicts.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence, editors' summary high: no frame, self-selected partly through harm-reduction channels, unknown response rate. Domain judgments agree, including 'partial yes' for items 3, 5, 6 and 8 with reasons (documented extension). Wilson intervals in the analysis field reproduce (water 111 of 116, 90.3-98.1; preloaded 32.8-50.5; postloaded 38.6-56.4), and the continuity-corrected frequency-postloading test gives p = 0.057 as stated.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the abstract generalizes awareness of harm to people who use ecstasy, rounds 38.8% to 'forty percent', and the Discussion's 'unlikely to cause harm' and Dutch death-reduction statements rest on no data and a newspaper report (p. 174). One fix: 'only from rodent studies with injected pre-treatments' should read 'most with injected pre-treatments' (p. 174).

missed: The paper glosses the 'comedown' as the acute recovery period (p. 169, Introduction 2nd paragraph); the claim's 'in the days after' is the editors' gloss, not the paper's.

Table 6 (p. 173): 21.8% of the 55 who gave reasons pre- or postloaded to increase the pleasurable effects of ecstasy (the third most common reason, above reducing side effects, 18.2%); the card has it in key finding 7, but the claim's magnitude omits it, so the claim presents pre- and postloading as purely protective in intent. The authors also raise the concern that people may keep or increase their use believing they are protected (p. 174, Discussion 12th paragraph).

The paper treats SSRIs inconsistently: p. 174 cites rat studies in which fluoxetine pre-treatment protected against MDMA's effects, while p. 175 lists SSRIs with 5-HTP and St John's wort as substances that 'augment the release of serotonin' and risk serotonin syndrome (SSRIs block reuptake). Not a number error; the claim's serotonin-syndrome line should stay attributed to the authors as a caution, with no data from the sample.

Shares among the 46, 54 and 55 respondents who listed products or reasons carry 95% intervals of about +/-12 to +/-14 points (for example 5-HTP before 41.3% of 46, Wilson 28.3-55.7%), wider than the +/-9 points the card and claim give for whole-sample shares.
